newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: China stalls for time on N.Korean defector.
newsitem.headline: China stalls for time on N.Korean defector.

text.p: Taken aback by the defection in Beijing of North Korea's top ideologue, China on Friday called for more time to resolve the crisis and urged both North and South Korea to stay calm.

North Koreans sporting trademark lapel pins of the late "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung waited in freezing temperatures outside a Seoul embassy compound, hoping Hwang Jang-yop would emerge and they could lure him home.
Hwang reportedly spent the day inside reading.

The drama that began on Wednesday when Hwang and an aide turned up in a taxi at the compound embarrassed China and raised fears of new tensions on the divided Korean peninsula, where two of the world's largest armies face each other.
The Hwang affair has compelled Beijing to choose between an old socialist comrade and a new capitalist friend, but despite a flurry of diplomatic activity there was no immediate solution.
In Singapore, Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and his South Korean counterpart Yoo Chong-ha met on the fringes of an Asia-Europe summit but failed to achieve a breakthrough.
"This incident happened all of a sudden, so we need more time to investigate," Qian told reporters.
He urged both Koreas "to treat this matter with a cool and calm manner, to keep peace and stability".
A South Korean official said he expected no resolution before the Singapore gathering ended on Saturday.
"It was the beginning of a useful discussion, but now it goes into diplomatic channels in Seoul and Beijing," said the official, who declined to be identified.

Talks were under way in Beijing between Chinese and South Korean officials, a Seoul embassy official said. Diplomats have said China may find itself with little option but to give in to the wishes of the defector.
Tokyo kept its distance, wary of acting as honest broker between the Koreas, which both have lingering hatred towards Japan, former colonial overlord of the Korean peninsula.
"We will watch the situation with great interest," top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference. "But will not go any further and get deeply involved."
Seoul regards the highest-level defection from the Stalinist North as a major coup that could produce a treasure trove of intelligence on a secretive government it fears is plotting its destruction.
For Pyongyang, the loss of the chief architect of its national ideology of Juche, a doctrine of fanatic self-reliance, is another blow on top of food shortages that are destabilising the country.

It is a slap in the face for Pyongyang's top leader Kim Jong-il, son of Kim Il-sung, whose 55th birthday celebrations on Sunday were intended to smooth the way for his formal accession to the posts of state president and general secretary of the ruling Worker's Party, analysts said.
Hwang was a close adviser to Kim Jong-il and one of 11 secretaries on the powerful secretariat of the Workers' Party.
In the sedate, tree-lined diplomatic district of Beijing, dozens of Chinese police cordoned Seoul's consular section off for a second day.

"They (North Koreans) are harassing us and we are a little nervous about that," said South Korean embassy spokesman Chang Moon Ik, adding that Seoul had asked Beijing to maintain tight security around the compound.
Hwang, who could face summary execution or a lifetime in the gulag if he goes back to the North, was in good health and sleeping well, Chang said. He spent the day reading.
A North Korean official standing outside the police cordon said Pyongyang had no plans to storm the compound to recover a countryman Pyongyang says was kidnapped.
"We are waiting here for him to come out and then ask him to come back," said the official.
"If China allows him to go to South Korea we will be disappointed," said another North Korean, one of a group of about 10 standing outside the building.
Some commentators have suggested Pyongyang might react violently to the defection of a man ranked 24 in its hierarchy who has now become its fiercest critic.
In letters released in South Korea, Hwang has lashed out at a system that he said has led to dictatorship and famine.
South and North Korea were separated at the end of World War Two and fought a war from 1950 to 1953. China fought on North Korea's side in the conflict.
